primer.may_p_world.title: The Maya kingdoms
primer.may_p_world.text: You were born in the land of the Maya, among dozens of city-kingdoms scattered through the rainforest. Each has its own k’uhul ajaw, a “holy lord”, and kings fight, intermarry or bow to whoever is strongest. The two great powers of this age are Tikal and Calakmul, capital of the Snake kingdom. Time is kept in the Long Count, a tally of days since the start of the present world in 3114 BC, and at the end of every twenty-year k’atun kings raise new carved stelae.
primer.may_p_world_550.title: The fall of Tikal
primer.may_p_world_550.text: In 562 Tikal, long the great power of the lowlands, suffered a crushing defeat by Caracol and its patron, the Snake kingdom. Tikal’s king Wak Chan K’awiil was probably sacrificed, and for more than a century Tikal almost stopped raising inscribed stelae. Meanwhile the Snake lords of Kaanul are rising: they gather allies and vassals across the region, and in 599 their army even sacked distant Palenque.
primer.may_p_world_600.title: The Snake kingdom’s hegemony
primer.may_p_world_600.text: Calakmul is the mightiest of the Maya kingdoms. Its great king Yuknoom Ch’een II (636–686) places his protégés on the thrones of many cities, Cancuen, Naranjo, Dos Pilas and La Corona among them, and collects their tribute. Tikal is surrounded but will not yield: in 657 a Calakmul army drove out its king, and in 679 Tikal was beaten by the Snake’s ally Dos Pilas. Meanwhile Pakal the Great rules Palenque (615–683), and Copan is ruled by the king scholars call Smoke Imix (628–695).
primer.may_p_world_696.title: Tikal reborn
primer.may_p_world_696.text: In 695 Tikal’s king Jasaw Chan K’awiil I defeated the army of Calakmul, capturing the enemy’s sacred palanquin, and celebrated with new temples. His son Yik’in Chan K’awiil smashes the Snake’s allies, and Calakmul’s star begins to fade. Peace does not follow, though: in 738 the unthinkable happened at Copan, whose king Waxaklajuun Ubaah K’awiil, known as “18 Rabbit”, was captured and beheaded by the ruler of little Quirigua nearby, once his own vassal.
primer.may_p_world_761.title: A crowded land
primer.may_p_world_761.text: The Maya land is more crowded than ever: tens of thousands of people live around the great cities, forests have been cleared for fields, and every ruler builds new temples. But wars multiply: in the 760s the kingdom of Dos Pilas collapsed, its last inhabitants throwing up walls right across their plazas. Noble families grow in number and demand their share of power and honour. Palenque’s last inscriptions date from around 800, and after the death of Copan’s king Yax Pasaj around 810 the carvers of Copan fall almost silent.
primer.may_p_world_830.title: The great abandonment
primer.may_p_world_830.text: The world of the Classic Maya is coming apart. One after another, cities stop raising stelae: Tikal’s last is dated 869, Calakmul’s around 900. Palaces empty, and people leave for the north, for Yucatan, or for small villages. No one knows for certain why; long droughts, exhausted soil, endless wars and lost faith in kings are all blamed, and most likely it was all of them together. Each new generation sees fewer festivals and more overgrown plazas.
primer.may_p_place.title: The land of the forest
primer.may_p_place.text: The Maya land is a flat limestone lowland covered in tropical forest, with mountains to the south. For half the year the rains pour; for the other half it is dry, the rivers shrink and water is worth more than anything. Howler monkeys roar and parrots screech in the forest, where jaguars, tapirs and deer roam. Cities sit among fields and groves, linked by raised white roads called sacbeob and by forest trails, and the next kingdom is several days away on foot.
primer.may_p_place_tikal.title: Tikal, called Mutul
primer.may_p_place_tikal.text: Its people call their kingdom Mutul, after an emblem glyph that looks like a tied knot of hair. Plastered temple-pyramids painted red rise above the forest canopy, and every great king builds a new one, taller than the last. Raised causeways link the city centre, and rainwater is caught in huge reservoirs: there is no river nearby, so through the dry season Tikal lives on its stores. For miles around stretch household yards with huts, kitchen gardens and maize fields.
primer.may_p_place_calakmul.title: Capital of the Snake kingdom
primer.may_p_place_calakmul.text: Calakmul sits on raised ground amid bajos, swamps that turn into shallow lakes in the rainy season. The Snake lords probably moved their capital here from Dzibanche only in the early 7th century, but they quickly made it the most feared city in the lowlands. Its great pyramid is one of the most massive in the Maya world, and more than a hundred stelae stand at the feet of its temples, more than anywhere else. White causeways run out to allied cities, and the kingdom’s emblem is a serpent’s head.
primer.may_p_place_palenque.title: Lakamha, “Big Water”
primer.may_p_place_palenque.text: Palenque sits on a green mountain ledge above the plain; streams run through the city, and one of them, the Otolum, was channelled through a stone tunnel beneath a plaza. Building here is unlike anywhere else: light, lofty vaults, delicate stucco reliefs, and a palace that will one day gain a tower. The city’s most famous king is K’inich Janaab Pakal, who took the throne at twelve in 615, reigned for 68 years and was laid to rest inside the pyramid of the Temple of the Inscriptions beneath a huge carved slab.
primer.may_p_place_copan.title: Copan, city of sculptors
primer.may_p_place_copan.text: Copan lies in a fertile river valley on the southeastern edge of the Maya world. Its dynasty was founded in 426 by a newcomer, K’inich Yax K’uk’ Mo’, and his descendants have held the throne ever since. Copan’s sculptors carve stelae so deeply that the kings on them look almost three-dimensional, and the Hieroglyphic Stairway, finished in 755, carries over two thousand glyphs, the longest Maya inscription. Scarlet macaws screech in the trees above the ballcourt.
primer.may_p_society.title: Lords and farmers
primer.may_p_society.text: At the top is the k’uhul ajaw, the holy lord, go-between for people and gods. Beneath him come the nobles: sajals who govern smaller towns for the king, scribes, war leaders and priests; as the era goes on there are more and more noble families, each demanding a bigger share. Most people, though, are farmers living in family groups around a shared yard: they pay tribute in maize, cloth and cacao and build the pyramids with their own hands. At the bottom are captives and slaves.
primer.may_p_society_slave.title: In bondage
primer.may_p_society_slave.text: You were born in bondage, among the lowest of the low. Little is known about Maya slavery in this era, but later accounts say slaves came from captured commoners, criminals and debtors. Noble captives meet a different fate: they are paraded before the people and sacrificed, while ordinary prisoners are put to work. They haul water, grind maize, and carry stone and lime to the temple building sites. A slave can be sold or given away, and sometimes bought back.
primer.may_p_society_peasant.title: A farming family
primer.may_p_society_peasant.text: You were born into a farming family. Your home is a hut of poles plastered with mud under a roof of palm leaves, standing on a stone platform around a yard shared with your relatives. Life revolves around the milpa, a plot where forest is burned off and maize is planted together with beans and squash. Farmers live by the rains: they sow when the wet season begins and harvest in autumn, and in the dry months they work on the king’s building projects and bring the lords tribute in cotton cloth and grain.
primer.may_p_society_noble.title: A noble house
primer.may_p_society_noble.text: You were born into a noble house, with stone rooms around a courtyard, servants and scribes of its own. The nobility take pride in family trees that run back to gods and famous ancestors; at festivals they wear jade, quetzal feathers and jaguar pelts. Boys learn writing, counting, ritual and war; girls learn weaving and ritual; and marriage is an alliance between houses, often from different kingdoms. A noble is bound to offer the gods their own blood, the most precious sacrifice of all.
primer.may_p_birth.title: Birth
primer.may_p_birth.text: Babies are born at home with a midwife; birth is watched over by the goddess of the moon and childbirth, whom later Maya will call Ix Chel. The day of birth in the sacred 260-day calendar matters greatly for the child’s fate and choice of name. Many infants have their heads bound tightly between boards so the skull grows long like the maize god’s, which is considered beautiful. Later accounts say a slight squint was admired too: a bead was tied to a child’s hair to dangle between the eyes.
primer.may_p_childhood.title: Childhood
primer.may_p_childhood.text: Your mother carries you on her back or her hip while she works. From about five, girls help grind maize on a stone metate, and boys carry firewood and scare birds away from the fields. Toys are clay whistles shaped like animals, little figurines and rubber balls. Noble children learn ritual, writing and counting from an early age. Later accounts say girls wore a shell at the waist and boys a white bead in their hair until they went through the coming-of-age rite.
primer.may_p_home.title: House and yard
primer.may_p_home.text: An ordinary home is a single room of poles and mud under a tall roof of palm thatch, set on a low platform so the rainy season does not flood it. Several houses of one family surround a shared yard with a three-stone hearth, a kitchen garden, fruit trees and turkeys. People sleep on mats and keep their things in baskets and clay pots. The dead are buried right under the house floor, so the ancestors stay close to the living.
primer.may_p_food.title: Maize, the flesh of people
primer.may_p_food.text: Maize is everything: legend says the gods shaped the first humans from maize dough. The kernels are boiled with lime, ground on a metate and made into tamales, dough parcels steamed in leaves, and thick atole porridge. Alongside come beans, squash, fiery chili and avocado, and at feasts venison, turkey and fattened dogs. Nobles drink cacao, a bitter frothy drink with chili, poured from one vessel to another until it foams. The cups even bear inscriptions: “drinking vessel for cacao of such-and-such lord”.
primer.may_p_clothes.title: Cotton, jade and feathers
primer.may_p_clothes.text: Men wear a cotton loincloth and a cloak; women a long skirt and a blouse. Cloth is woven on a backstrap loom and dyed red, yellow, blue and black. Nobles adorn themselves with jade ear spools and necklaces, and at festivals wear towering headdresses of shimmering quetzal feathers. Many people file their teeth and inlay them with jade, paint their bodies and wear tattoos. The more ornaments you wear, the higher your rank.
primer.may_p_faith.title: Gods and blood
primer.may_p_faith.text: The Maya picture thirteen heavens above the earth and nine layers of underworld below, with the earth itself floating on the back of a vast creature. The gods of maize, of rain (Chaak), of the sun (K’inich) and the old creator Itzamnaaj demand nourishment: fragrant copal incense, blood and, on the greatest days, human life. Time is sacred: the 260-day calendar tells which days are lucky, and priests count the cycles by which the gods return. Caves are doorways to the other world.
primer.may_p_faith_noble.title: The blood of lords
primer.may_p_faith_noble.text: For nobles, faith is a duty. On great days the king and his wife offer their blood to the gods: he pierces his flesh with a stingray spine, she draws a thorned cord through her tongue, and the drops fall onto bark paper that is burned in a bowl. In the smoke, the Maya believe, the Vision Serpent appears with an ancestor or a god in its jaws. That is exactly how Queen K’abal Xook is shown on a carved lintel at Yaxchilan. Nobles dance in the masks of gods and keep count of the k’atuns, marking each with a new stela.
primer.may_p_work.title: Cacao instead of money
primer.may_p_work.text: The Maya have no coins: payment seems to be made in cacao beans, lengths of cotton cloth and beads of jade and shell. Most work is in the fields; craftsmen carve jade, paint vessels, weave, and knap blades from obsidian brought down from the highlands. There are no pack animals or carts, so porters carry loads on their backs, and canoes travel the rivers and coasts with salt, obsidian and feathers. The nobility collect tribute in cloth, cacao and labour.
primer.may_p_law.title: The lords’ justice
primer.may_p_law.text: No written laws survive from the Maya of this era: justice is dispensed by the ruler, his governors and the elders of each lineage. What we know of their customs comes from later accounts: a thief had to repay what he stole, or become a slave if he could not; a killing was paid for with a life or with compensation to the victim’s family. The worst crime is betraying your lord. Disputes over land and water were probably settled within the lineage by its elders, and a noble’s word weighed more than a commoner’s.
primer.may_p_health.title: Herbs and sweat baths
primer.may_p_health.text: Healers treat the sick with herbs, bloodletting, steam and incantations, for illness here is the anger of the gods, a curse or a broken vow. Many cities have stone sweat baths: water is poured over hot stones and people sit in the steam to purify themselves, and perhaps also after childbirth. Diarrhoea and fevers of the rainy season carry off the most children; famine years take the adults. The dead are buried with a jade bead or maize kernels in the mouth, so they will have something to eat in the next world.
primer.may_p_women.title: A woman’s lot
primer.may_p_women.text: From childhood a girl learns to weave on a backstrap loom, grind maize and cook: a woman spends hours every day at the metate and the hearth. Girls marry young; later accounts say a groom sometimes worked for years for his bride’s family. The cloth women weave is real wealth, paid as tribute and given to gods and noble guests. A woman is honoured as the mother of the lineage, and the moon, weaving and childbirth all belong to her.
primer.may_p_women_noble.title: Maya queens
primer.may_p_women_noble.text: Noble Maya women are far more than wives: their marriages seal alliances between kingdoms, and they appear on stelae beside their husbands. Lady Yohl Ik’nal ruled Palenque in her own right from 583 to 604. A princess of Dos Pilas, Lady Six Sky, arrived in Naranjo in 682 to revive its dynasty and for years held power and waged war on behalf of her young son. Noblewomen lead rituals, and their textiles and jewels are marks of authority.
primer.may_p_leisure.title: Ball games and festivals
primer.may_p_leisure.text: The greatest spectacle is the ball game: a heavy rubber ball is struck with the hips and a padded torso, and touching it with the hands is forbidden. The game is sacred, echoing the legendary contest of the Hero Twins against the lords of the underworld, and sometimes it ends with the sacrifice of captives. At festivals drums, conch-shell trumpets and flutes ring out, masked dancers play gods and animals, and the adults drink intoxicating brews of honey, maize and bark.
primer.may_p_knowledge.title: Writing and numbers
primer.may_p_knowledge.text: The Maya have the most sophisticated writing system in the Americas. Scribes paint with brushes in folding books of fig-bark paper and carve inscriptions in stone, using more than eight hundred signs, some for syllables and some for whole words. They count in twenties: a dot is one, a bar is five, and a special sign stands for zero, an idea the Maya came up with on their own, one of very few peoples to do so. Astronomers predict eclipses and track the cycle of Venus, and scribes are honoured as favourites of the gods.
primer.may_p_war.title: War for captives
primer.may_p_war.text: Maya wars are more often raids than conquests: the main goal is to seize an enemy king or noble warriors, bring them home and present them to the gods. Warriors fight with flint-tipped spears and clubs edged with obsidian, protected by shields and quilted cotton armour. Fighting usually happens in the dry season, once the harvest is in. Kings boast of titles like “he of twenty captives”, and behind the small wars looms the great rivalry between Tikal and Calakmul.
